nodes.name: unexpected plane curve (CHMN)
nodes.statement: Given a finite set of points $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ with $n=2$, we say that plane curves of degree $d=m+1$ containing $Z$ and having a general point of multiplicity $m$ are {\it unexpected} when such curves exist but the conditions imposed by vanishing to order $m$ at $P$ on the vector space of forms of degree $d$ vanishing on $Z$ are not independent.
nodes.statement_short: Plane curves of degree m+1 through Z with a general point of multiplicity m are unexpected when they exist although the multiplicity conditions are dependent.

nodes.name: ground field K
nodes.statement: To describe the problem and our approach to it in a more precise way, let $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0.

nodes.name: homogeneous coordinate ring R
nodes.statement: Let $R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n]=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ be the homogeneous coordinate ring of $n$-dimensional projective space.

nodes.name: fat point scheme mP
nodes.statement: Consider a general point $P\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$. The fat point scheme $X=mP$ is the scheme defined by the homogeneous ideal $I_X=(I_{P})^{m} \subset R$, where $I_{P}$ is the ideal generated by all forms that vanish at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: The fat point scheme X=mP at a general point P is defined by the m-th power of the ideal of P.

nodes.name: degree-d component [I]_d
nodes.statement: Given a homogeneous ideal $I\subseteq R$, we denote by $[I]_d$ the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$-vector space spanned by homogeneous forms in $I$ of degree $d$.

nodes.name: dimension of forms through a fat point
nodes.statement: It is well known and easy to show that $\dim_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}}[I_X]_d=\max(0,\binom{n+d}{n}-\binom{m-1+n}{n})$.
conclusions: $\dim_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}}[I_X]_d=\max(0,\binom{n+d}{n}-\binom{m-1+n}{n})$

nodes.name: reduced point scheme Z
nodes.statement: Given distinct points $Q_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, we define $Z=Q_1+\cdots +Q_s$ to be the subscheme defined by the ideal $I_Z=\cap_jI_{Q_j}\subset R$.

nodes.name: unexpected hypersurface
nodes.statement: We say that $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ {\em admits an unexpected hypersurface} with respect to $X$ of degree $d$ if $$\dim [I_Z\cap I_X]_d > \max \left \{ 0, \dim [I_Z]_d-\binom{m-1+n}{n} \right \}.$$ That is, $Z$ admits an unexpected hypersurface with respect to $X$ of degree $d$ if the conditions imposed by $X$ on forms of degree $d$ vanishing on $Z$ are not independent. We will also sometimes say that $Z$ admits an unexpected hypersurface with a general point $P$ of multiplicity~$m$.
nodes.genus: hypersurface of degree $d$ containing $Z$ with a general point of multiplicity $m$
differentia: the conditions imposed by $X$ on forms of degree $d$ vanishing on $Z$ are not independent
nodes.statement_short: Z admits an unexpected hypersurface of degree d w.r.t. X=mP if dim[I_Z∩I_X]_d exceeds max(0, dim[I_Z]_d − binom(m−1+n,n)).

nodes.name: classification of unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: Characterize and then classify all quadruples $(n,d,m,Z)$ where $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ admits an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Characterize and classify all (n,d,m,Z) with Z admitting an unexpected hypersurface of degree d with a general point of multiplicity m.
nodes.label: prob:intro

nodes.name: existence of unexpected hypersurfaces (classification of (n,d,m))
nodes.statement: Given positive integers $(n,d,m)$ with $n>1$, there exists an unexpected hypersurface for some finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of degree $d$ with a general point of multiplicity $m$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds: \begin{enumerate}[label={(\roman*)}] \item[(i)] $n=2$ and $(d,m)$ satisfies $d > m > 2$; or \item[(ii)] $n \ge 3$ and $(d,m)$ satisfies $d \geq m \geq 2$. \end{enumerate}
also_stated_at: \ \begin{enumerate}[label={(\roman*)}] \item There exists a finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ admitting an unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point if and only if $d > m > 2$. \item For $n \geq 3$, there exists a finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ admitting an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point if and only if $d \geq m \geq 2$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: positive integers $(n,d,m)$ with $n>1$
conclusions: there exists an unexpected hypersurface for some finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of degree $d$ with a general point of multiplicity $m$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds
equivalent_conditions: there exists an unexpected hypersurface for some finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of degree $d$ with a general point of multiplicity $m$
nodes.statement_short: Unexpected hypersurfaces of degree d with a general m-fold point exist in P^n iff d>m>2 (n=2) or d≥m≥2 (n≥3).
nodes.label: mainThm

nodes.name: saturated ideal I_V and ideal sheaf
nodes.statement: For any subvariety (or subscheme) $V \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ we write $I_V \subseteq R$ for the saturated ideal of $V$ and $\mathcal{I}_V$ for the sheaf on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ corresponding to $I_V$.

nodes.name: first difference of a function
nodes.statement: For any integer function $h : \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ the first difference $\Delta h$ is the backward difference $\Delta h(t) = h(t)-h(t-1)$, where we make the convention $h(-1)=0$ (so $\Delta h(0) = h(0)$).

nodes.name: cone with vertex P
nodes.statement: By a cone with vertex $P$ we mean a scheme $X$ such that for every point $Q$ in $X$ the line joining $P$ and $Q$ is in $X$.
differentia: for every point $Q$ in $X$ the line joining $P$ and $Q$ is in $X$

nodes.name: hypersurfaces with a point of full multiplicity are cones
nodes.statement: In particular, by B\'ezout, every hypersurface of degree $d$ with a point of multiplicity $d$ at a point $P$ is a cone with vertex $P$.
assumptions: every hypersurface of degree $d$ with a point of multiplicity $d$ at a point $P$
conclusions: is a cone with vertex $P$

nodes.name: plane curves in P^3 admit no unexpected cone
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that a plane curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ does not admit an unexpected hypersurface with a point of multiplicity $d$ -- instead, a point of multiplicity $d$ imposes the expected number of conditions on hypersurfaces of degree $d$ containing the plane curve (use the fact that a plane curve in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ is a complete intersection, and the known Hilbert function for complete intersections).
assumptions: a plane curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$
conclusions: does not admit an unexpected hypersurface with a point of multiplicity $d$
nodes.statement_short: A plane curve of degree d in P^3 has no unexpected surface with a d-fold point (complete-intersection Hilbert function).

nodes.name: cone over a non-degenerate space curve is unexpected
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ ($C$ may be reducible, disconnected, and/or singular but note that $d \geq 2$ since $C$ is non-degenerate, with $C$ being two skew lines if $d=2$). Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point. Then the cone $S_P=S_P(C)$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $C$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. It is the unique unexpected surface of this degree and multiplicity.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$
Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point.
conclusions: the cone $S_P=S_P(C)$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $C$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$
It is the unique unexpected surface of this degree and multiplicity.
nodes.statement_short: For a reduced non-degenerate space curve C of degree d, the cone over C from a general point is the unique unexpected degree-d surface with a d-fold point.
nodes.label: cone in P3

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement:
We first check uniqueness. Let $F$ be a form defining a surface containing $C$, of degree $d$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. Let $\lambda$ be a line through $P$ and any point $Q$, of $C$. Then by B'ezout, $F$ must vanish on all of $\lambda$. Thus the surface defined by $F$ is precisely $S_P$. We now check unexpectedness. Let $D$ be a smooth plane curve of degree $d$. \medskip 
oindent \underline{Claim 1}: {\em The arithmetic genus, $g_C$, of $C$ is strictly less than that of $D$, which is $g_D =  inom{d-1}{2}$. } \medskip This argument is classical. Much of it is given in \cite{harris} (when C is irreducible) and in \cite{migbook} Proposition 1.4.2, so no claim is made to originality; we include it here just for the reader's convenience. Let $\Gamma$ be a general hyperplane section of $C$ by a hyperplane $H$ defined by a general linear form $L$. Let $I_{\Gamma | H}$ be the saturated ideal of $\Gamma$ in $H$. Let $\ell \gg 0$. Then \[  egin{array}{rcl} d\ell - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(\ell)) \ & = & h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \end{array} \] where $h_{R/I_C}(t)$ is the Hilbert function of $C$. On the other hand, for any integer $t$ we have the exact sequence \[  egin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & ightarrow & [I_C]_{t-1} & ightarrow & [I_C]_t & ightarrow & [I_{\Gamma|H} ]_t & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_C(t-1)) & ightarrow & \dots \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & 
earrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \ &&&&&&& [K]_t \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } 
earrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \ \end{array} \] (where $K$ is just the cokernel). Then after adding and subtracting some binomial coefficients and setting $ ar R = R/L$, we obtain \[  egin{array}{rcl} \Delta h_{R/I_C} (t) & = & h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}}(t) + \dim [K]_t \ & \geq & h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t). \end{array} \] So since $\ell \gg 0$ we obtain \[  egin{array}{rcl} g_C & = & 1 + d\ell - h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \ & = & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell \Delta h_{R/I_C}(t) \ & \leq & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \ & = & \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t) ight ]. \end{array} \] Now replace $C$ by $D$, and replace $\Gamma$ by the hyperplane section of $D$, which is a set of $d$ collinear points, say $A$. We have, similarly, \[ g_D = \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{ ar R/I_A}(t) ight ] =  inom{d-1}{2} . \] It is clear that for any $t \geq 1$ we have \[ h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \geq h_{ ar R/I_A}(t) \] with strict inequality for $t=1$, so we obtain $g_C < g_D$. This completes the proof of Claim 1. Now, by \cite{GLP} Remark (1) (p. 497), we have $H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0$, and we also have $H^1(\mathcal I_D(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_D(d)) = 0$. Consider the exact sequence \[ 0 ightarrow [I_C]_d ightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3}(d)) ightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) ightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) ightarrow 0. \] \medskip 
oindent \underline{Claim 2}: {\em Let $D$ be a plane curve of degree $d$. Then $h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d))$.} \medskip Indeed, \[  egin{array}{rcl} d^2 - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^1(\mathcal O_C(d)) \ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) \ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) \end{array} \] and similarly for $D$, so thanks to Claim 1 we have \[ h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \] and we have Claim 2. Then \[  egin{array}{rcll} \dim [I_C]_d & = & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) & \hbox{(since } h^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0 ) \ \ & < & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \end{array} \] thanks to Claim 2. To check that $S_P$ is an unexpected surface it is enough to note that \[  egin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_C]_d -  inom{d-1+3}{3} & < & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) -  inom{d-1+3}{3} \ \ & = & \displaystyle  inom{d+2}{2} - [d^2 - g_D + 1] \ \ & = & 1 \end{array} \] using the value of $g_D$ mentioned above.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by Bézout; unexpectedness by comparing h^0(O_C(d)) with that of a plane curve via the genus bound g_C<g_D. Key step: Claim 1, the genus bound from Hilbert functions of hyperplane sections.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.4
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on $n$. The initial case is Proposition \ref{cone in P3}, so we can assume $n \geq 4$. Let $H$ be a general hyperplane through $P$ and let $W = V \cap H$. Since $P$ is general, we can assume that $H$ is general as well. By Lemma \ref{nondeg}, $W$ is non-degenerate in $H = \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$, and it is also reduced and equidimensional. Let $T_P$ be the cone in $H$ over $W$ with vertex $P$. Thus by induction, $T_P$ is the unique hypersurface of degree $d$ containing $W$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$, and it is unexpected. Consider the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_V]_{d-1} & \rightarrow & [I_V]_d & \rightarrow & [I_{W|H} ]_d & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_V(d-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_d \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] We have \[ \dim [I_V]_d = \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \dim [K]_d. \] We claim that \[ \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \leq 0 \] so that $S_P$ is unexpected. We have \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \left ( \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} \right ) \\ \\ && \displaystyle + \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \\ \\ & \leq & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \binom{d+n-2}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} - \binom{d+n-2}{n} - \dim [K]_d . \end{array} \] But Remark \ref{low deg rmk} gives \[ \dim [I_V]_{d-1} \leq \binom{d+n-2}{n}, \] which completes the claim. Uniqueness follows in the same way as it did for Proposition~\ref{cone in P3}.

nodes.name: fewer points suffice
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{curves 1}, Corollary \ref{curves 2}, Corollary \ref{add S} and Corollary \ref{WLP Pn cons} all deal with the situation that we begin with a set of points lying on a variety $C$ of codimension two in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, and have enough points so that $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$. In fact this assumption can be relaxed, although the statement becomes a little bit less transparent so we retained this assumption. But notice that the fact that $C$ already admits an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ means that we only need a set of $\binom{d+n}{n} - \binom{d-1+n}{n}$ points on $C$ that impose independent conditions on forms of degree $d$, and this number can be much smaller than the number forced by the condition $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$. For example, say $C$ is a general smooth rational curve in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ of degree 6. The Hilbert function of $C$ is given by the sequence $1,4,10, 19, 25, 31, 37, \dots$ so the assumption that $[I_C]_6 = [I_Z]_6$ means we need $Z$ to have at least 37 points of $C$. Instead, suppose that $Z$ is a sufficiently general set of $\binom{6+3}{3} - \binom{5+3}{3} = 28$ points on $C$. Then the Hilbert function of $Z$ is given by the sequence $1,4,10,19, 25, 28, 28, \dots$ and we still do not expect a hypersurface of degree 6 with a point of multiplicity 6 to contain $Z$, but we know that the cone over $C$ is such a hypersurface. Notice that in this case we not only have $[I_C]_6 \neq [I_Z]_6$ but even $[I_C]_5 \neq [I_Z]_5$.

nodes.name: general points admit no unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is not the case that all sets of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ (or any other projective space) admit an unexpected surface (resp. hypersurface) of some sort. Indeed, suppose $Z$ is a general set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ and let us ask if there is any degree and multiplicity at a general point, in which $Z$ admits an unexpected surface. By considering the conditions imposed first by the general multiple point and then by the general points $Z$, we see that we must always get the expected number of conditions. What is interesting is that in \cite{CHMN} Corollary 6.8 it was shown that a set of points in linear general position in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ does not admit an unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $d-1$ at a general point. Example \ref{twc1} already shows that this does not extend to a set of points in linear general position in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$, if we weaken the condition on the multiplicity to allow multiplicity $d$. We do not know if the precise result from \cite{CHMN} continues to hold in higher dimensional projective spaces.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.15 (= Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement: For (i), we first note that there is an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point for each $m \geq 3$. Indeed, \begin{itemize} \item $m \leq 2$. It was shown by Akesseh \cite{A} that this occurs only in characteristic 2. (See also \cite{FGST} for a different proof that shows that it does not occur in characteristic zero.) \item $m=3$. This comes from the dual of the $B_3$ arrangement \cite{DIV}. \item $m=4$. Consider the line arrangement defined by the linear factors of $$xyz(x^3-y^3)(x^3-z^3)(y^3-z^3).$$ This is a supersolvable arrangement (see definition in \S\ref{root system section}), so Theorem 3.7 of \cite{DMO} applies. In particular, the dual points give a reduced set of 12 points which admit an unexpected curve with $d=5$ and $m=4$. \item $m=5$. This follows from \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $k=2$. \item $m \geq 6$. This comes from the points dual to the Fermat arrangement, by \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $t \geq 5$. \end{itemize} \noindent It is clear that a set of points $Z$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ cannot admit an unexpected curve whose degree and multiplicity at a general point $P$ are equal (unlike what we have seen in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$). Indeed, in this situation the line joining $P$ to any point of $Z$ must be a component of such an unexpected curve, so the unexpected curve is a cone with vertex $P$ over the points of $Z$. Let $d = \deg Z$ be the degree of this curve. Then $Z$ imposes independent conditions on curves of degree $d$, so $\dim [I_Z]_d = \binom{d+2}{2} - d$. Then \[ \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{(d-1)+2}{2} = \binom{d+2}{2} - d - \binom{d+1}{2} = (d+1)-d = 1 \] so in fact the cone is not unexpected. Thus $m < d$. Since $P$ is general, it does not lie on $A$. Then choosing sufficiently many points on $A$ gives a unique unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at $P$. (A similar construction also was used in \cite[Proposition 6.7]{DIV}, but see \cite[Example 7.4]{CHMN}.) Part (ii) follows from Proposition \ref{Pn} and Corollary \ref{add S}.

nodes.name: Weak and Strong Lefschetz Properties
nodes.statement: Let $R/I$ be an artinian $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$-algebra and let $L$ be a general linear form. Then $R/I$ satisfies the {\em Weak Lefschetz Property (WLP)} in degree $i$ if $\times L : [R/I]_i \rightarrow [R/I]_{i+1}$ has maximal rank, and we say that $R/I$ satisfies the {\em Strong Lefschetz Property (SLP)} in degree $i$ with range $k$ if $\times L^k : [R/I]_i \rightarrow [R/I]_{i+k}$ has maximal rank. We say that $R/I$ satisfies WLP (resp.\ SLP) if it does so for all $i$ (resp. for all $i$ and $k$).

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.20
nodes.statement: We recall that we can always find an irreducible, non-degenerate subvariety $V$ of codimension 2 and degree $k$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$. In fact, if $k$ is even we take $V$ as an intersection of a general form of degree $\frac{k}{2}$ and a general quadric. If $k$ is odd we take $V$ as a general arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay subscheme with a minimal free resolution of the form \[ 0 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+3}{2} })^2 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+1}{2} })^2 \oplus R(-2) \rightarrow R \rightarrow R/I_V \rightarrow 0 \] (obtained, for example, by linking from a linear space of codimension 2 using the complete intersection of a quadric and a form of degree $\frac{k+1}{2}$). Using this sequence, or the Koszul resolution if $k$ is even, we obtain \[ \dim [R/I_V]_k = f (n, k). \] Since $V$ is irreducible, it makes sense to speak of a general set of points on $V$. Let $Z$ be a general set of $N$ points on $V$. From the generality of $Z$ we have \[ \dim [R/I_Z]_k = \min \{ \dim [R/I_V]_k , |Z| \}, \] hence $\dim [I_V]_k = \dim [I_Z]_k$. By Proposition 2.4 we then have that the cone over $V$ with vertex at a general point $P$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $k$ and multiplicity $k$ at $P$. Then the argument in the proof of Corollary 2.16 can be extended to our situation to show that the multiplication from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$ by a general linear form has an unexpectedly large cokernel, i.e. maximal rank does not hold. Since $Z$ is general on $V$ and $V$ is irreducible and non-degenerate, $Z$ is a set of points in linear general position, and this implies the condition on the linear forms not to have a common zero.

Then there exists an ideal $I = (L_1^d,\dots, L_e^d)$ (for suitable $e$) for which \[ \times L^{d-m+1} : [R/I]_{m-1} \rightarrow [R/I]_d \] fails to have maximal rank if and only if one of the following holds. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] We have $n = 2$ and $d > m > 2$. \item[(ii)] We have $n \geq 3$ and $d \geq m \geq 2$. \end{itemize} In both cases this means that $R/I$ fails the SLP in degree $m-1$ and range $d-m+1$.
assumptions: Let $R = \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\dots,x_n]$.
Fix positive integers $d\geq m$.
conclusions: there exists an ideal $I = (L_1^d,\dots, L_e^d)$ (for suitable $e$) for which \[ \times L^{d-m+1} : [R/I]_{m-1} \rightarrow [R/I]_d \] fails to have maximal rank if and only if one of the following holds.
equivalent_conditions: there exists an ideal $I = (L_1^d,\dots, L_e^d)$ (for suitable $e$) for which \[ \times L^{d-m+1} : [R/I]_{m-1} \rightarrow [R/I]_d \] fails to have maximal rank

nodes.name: failure of maximal rank and Schenck-Seceleanu
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Note that Corollary \ref{fail SLP} (and similarly for the earlier results) is not necessarily about failure of surjectivity. The proof only shows that the cokernel of $\times L^{d-m+1}$ is bigger than expected, which means failure of surjectivity if $\dim [R/I]_{m-1} \geq \dim [R/I]_d$, and it means failure of injectivity if $\dim [R/I]_{m-1} \leq \dim [R/I]_d$. \item In \cite{SS}, Schenck and Seceleanu proved the striking result that for {\em every} ideal of the form $I = (L_1^{a_1},\dots,L_e^{a_e})$ in the ring $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x,y,z]$, the quotient $R/I$ has the WLP. In the case that all $a_i$ are equal to some $d$, we can recover this result from Corollary \ref{fail SLP}. Indeed, this is the case $n=2$. Checking whether WLP holds amounts to considering the case $m=d$ (since we are studying $\times L^1$), and Corollary \ref{fail SLP} says that in this case maximal rank always holds. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The cokernel is only shown to be too big; Corollary 2.21 recovers the Schenck-Seceleanu WLP theorem for equal powers in three variables.

assumptions: {\em every} ideal of the form $I = (L_1^{a_1},\dots,L_e^{a_e})$ in the ring $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x,y,z]$
conclusions: the quotient $R/I$ has the WLP

nodes.name: simplicial real line arrangement
nodes.statement: It is a simplicial real arrangement. (This means that the lines divide the real projective plane into triangles.)

nodes.name: Melchior's inequality
nodes.statement: (If $t_k$ denotes the number of points where exactly $k$ lines meet, an inequality of Melchior \cite{Me} for real arrangements of $d>2$ lines with $t_d=0$ states that $t_2\geq 3+\sum_{k>2}(k-3)t_k$.
assumptions: $t_k$ denotes the number of points where exactly $k$ lines meet
real arrangements of $d>2$ lines with $t_d=0$

nodes.name: free line arrangement
nodes.statement: It is free (meaning that if $F$ is the product of the linear forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$, then there are no second syzygies for the Jacobian ideal $J_F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$; i.e., the syzygy bundle for $J_F$ is free.)
nodes.statement_short: An arrangement is free if the Jacobian ideal of its defining product has no second syzygies (free syzygy bundle).

nodes.name: supersolvable line arrangement and modular point
nodes.statement: A line arrangement in the projective plane is {\em supersolvable} if there is a so-called {\em modular} point, i.e., a point $P$ where two or more of the lines meet such that if $Q$ is any other point where two or more of the lines meet, then the line through $P$ and $Q$ is a line in the arrangement.
nodes.genus: line arrangement in the projective plane
differentia: there is a so-called {\em modular} point, i.e., a point $P$ where two or more of the lines meet such that if $Q$ is any other point where two or more of the lines meet, then the line through $P$ and $Q$ is a line in the arrangement

nodes.name: multiplicity of a point for a line arrangement
nodes.statement: The {\em multiplicity} of a point with respect to a line arrangement is just the number of lines in the arrangement containing the point.

nodes.name: points of maximum multiplicity in supersolvable arrangements are modular
nodes.statement: When a line arrangement is supersolvable, every point of maximum multiplicity is modular (but not every modular point need have maximum multiplicity) \cite{AT} (only the arXiv version includes the proof).
assumptions: When a line arrangement is supersolvable
conclusions: every point of maximum multiplicity is modular

nodes.name: Di Marca-Malara-Oneto criterion for supersolvable arrangements
nodes.statement: The result of \cite{DMO} says the point scheme $Z_A$ dual to the lines of a supersolvable line arrangement $A$ has an unexpected curve of degree $m_A$ with respect to $X=(m_A-1)P$ for a general point $P$ if and only if $2m_A<d_A$, where $d_A$ is the number of lines in the arrangement and $m_A$ is the maximum multiplicity of a point for $A$, and in this case the unexpected curve is unique.
assumptions: the point scheme $Z_A$ dual to the lines of a supersolvable line arrangement $A$
$d_A$ is the number of lines in the arrangement and $m_A$ is the maximum multiplicity of a point for $A$
conclusions: has an unexpected curve of degree $m_A$ with respect to $X=(m_A-1)P$ for a general point $P$ if and only if $2m_A<d_A$
in this case the unexpected curve is unique
equivalent_conditions: has an unexpected curve of degree $m_A$ with respect to $X=(m_A-1)P$ for a general point $P$
nodes.statement_short: Dual points of a supersolvable arrangement have a (unique) unexpected curve of degree m_A with an (m_A−1)-fold general point iff 2m_A<d_A.

nodes.name: B_3 points have a unique unexpected quartic
nodes.statement: Since $m_{B_3}=4$ and $d_{B_3}=9$, it follows that $Z_{B_3}$ has a unique unexpected curve of degree 4.
conclusions: $Z_{B_3}$ has a unique unexpected curve of degree 4

nodes.name: roots of B_3
nodes.statement: The roots of $B_3$ can be defined as the integer vector solutions $(a,b,c)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^3$ to $1\leq a^2+b^2+c^2\leq2$.

nodes.name: point set Z_A of a root system
nodes.statement: The set-up then is: a root system $A$ gives a finite set of vectors of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$ for some $n$. Each root gives a point in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$ and the set of these points for the given root system $A$ gives the point set we denote by $Z_A$.

nodes.name: hyperplane arrangement of a root system
nodes.statement: The codimension 1 linear subspaces normal to the roots define the hyperplanes of the arrangement corresponding to $A$ which we also refer to by $A$.

nodes.name: dual point set Z_A of a line arrangement
nodes.statement: Results of \cite{DIV} and \cite{FV} show that it is useful in this situation to regard a point set $Z$ as the points $Z_{\mathcal{A}}$ dual to a line arrangement $\mathcal{A}$.

nodes.name: generic point and ring S
nodes.statement: In principle, given a finite set of points $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ and a general point $P=[a_0:\cdots:a_n]$, to find an unexpected hypersurface for $Z+mP$ computationally one takes $P$ to be the generic point $P=[1:\frac{a_1}{a_0}:\cdots:\frac{a_n}{a_0}]$ and works as usual in the homogeneous coordinate ring $S=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[x_0,\ldots,x_n]= \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})}]$. (We will however abuse notation and typically use $[a_0:\cdots:a_n]$ to denote $P$ and refer to it as a general point.)
nodes.statement_short: Treat a general point as the generic point over K(a_1/a_0,…,a_n/a_0) and work in the polynomial ring S over that field.

nodes.name: bi-graded ring R
nodes.statement: However, it can be convenient and more efficient to work in the bi-graded ring $R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n][x_0,\ldots,x_n]$.

nodes.name: F^* (bi-homogeneous numerator of F)
nodes.statement: Thus given a form $F\in S$ of degree $d$ but which is not in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$, there is (up to scalars in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$) a unique factorization $F=BG/H$, where $B$ and $H$ are relatively prime forms in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n]$ and $G\in R$ is bi-homogeneous with no factors of bi-degree $(a,0)$ with $a>0$; its bi-degree is $(t,d)$, where $t=\deg(H)-\deg(B)$. We denote $G$ by $F^*$.
nodes.statement_short: F^* is the bi-homogeneous factor G of F=BG/H with no pure-a factors; it has bi-degree (t,d).

nodes.name: G° (dehomogenization of G)
nodes.statement: Given any bi-homogeneous element $G\in R$ of bi-degree $(t,d)$, we denote $G/a_0^t$ by $G^\circ$. Note that $G^\circ\in S$ is homogeneous of degree $d$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: (a) Since $F=BF^*/H=B(F^*)^\circ a_0^t/H$, where $t=\deg(H)-\deg(B)$, we see that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by $Ba_0^t/H$, which is a unit in $S$. (b) Note that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by a unit factor in $S$, so one is irreducible if and only if the other is. Also, $F^*$ by construction has no factors of bi-degree $(f,0)$ with $f>0$, so if $F^*$ fails to be irreducible, it factors as $F^*=AB$ where $A$ and $B$ have bi-degree $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$ with $d_A,d_B>0$ and $d_A+d_B=d$. But then $(F^*)^\circ=A^\circ B^\circ$ is a product of factors of positive degree and hence not irreducible. (c) If $G^\circ$ is not irreducible, then $G^\circ=AB$ where both $A$ and $B$ have positive degree $d_A$ and $d_B$, so we have $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ where $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have bi-degrees $(t_\alpha,0)$ and $(t_\beta,0)$. Since $R$ is a UFD, the denominators in the right hand side of the expression $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ must cancel with factors of the numerators of the expression $\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ and this does not affect the values of $d_A$ or $d_B$, so we may assume that $\alpha,\beta, A^*, B^*$ all are in $R$ and $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a',d_A)$ and $(b',d_B)$, where the simplification might have changed $a$ and $b$ but will have left $d_a$ and $d_B$ unchanged. Since $d_A$ and $d_B$ are both positive, $G$ has nonunit factors so $G$ is not irreducible. Now note that irreducibility of $G^\circ$ implies that for $(G^\circ)^*$ by (b). Finally, by construction, if $G$ is irreducible with bi-degree $(t,d)$ where $d>0$, then $G=c(G^\circ)^*$ for some nonzero $c\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$, hence $(G)=((G^\circ)^*)$. (d) Since $F\in I_{mP}$, by (a) we have $\frac{F^*}{a_0^s}=(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$, where $(s,d)$ is the bi-degree of $F^*$, and since $d$ is the degree of $(F^*)^\circ$ and since $(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$ we have $d\geq m$. Now let $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= F^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)=\frac{F^*(a_0,\ldots,a_n,x_0,\ldots,x_n)}{a_0^sx_0^d},$$ so as a rational function $D$ has bi-degree $(0,0)$, but as a polynomial in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}]$, $D$ has degree $\delta\leq d$. Moreover, since $x_0\not\in I_P$, we have $D\in I_{mQ}$ where $Q$ is the point $Q=(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})$ in the affine open subset $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})^n$ away from $x_0=0$. Now translate $Q$ to the origin; i.e., consider $$H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big).$$ Note that $$a_0^{s+d}x_0^dH=a_0^{s+d}x_0^dF^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)=$$ $$F^*\big(a_0,\ldots,a_n,a_0x_0,a_0x_1+a_1x_0,\ldots,a_0x_n+a_nx_0\big)\in R$$ is a bi-homogeneous polynomial of bi-degree $(s+d,d)$. Since $H$ has multiplicity $m$ at the origin (with respect to the variables $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$), $H$ is a sum of terms where each term consists of a monomial in $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$ of degree at least $m$ and at most $d$, times a polynomial in the variables $\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}$ of degree at most $s+d$. Thus each term is of the form $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ where $m\leq \sum_ji_j\leq d$ and $c$ has degree at most $s+d$. Thus multiplying by $a_0^{s+d}x_0^d$ clears the denominators. Translating back we recover $D$; i.e., $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big),$$ but each term becomes $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)^{i_n} =c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{a_0x_1-a_1x_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{a_0x_n-a_nx_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ and multiplying by $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^d$ we obtain $$C(a_0,\ldots,a_n)(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}$$ where $C$ is homogeneous in the variables $a_i$ of degree $s+d$, and $$(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}\in J_{mP}.$$ Thus $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dH\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)= a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dD=a_0^{2d}F^*\in J_{mP}$. But by \cite[Corollary 7.10]{BV}, since $J_P$ is the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix of indeterminates, namely the two sets of variables, the powers $J_{mP}$ are primary for $J_P$. Since no power of $a_0$ is in $J_{mP}$, we see that $F^*\in J_{mP}$. (e) If $G\in J_{mP}$, then $G=\sum_s H_sM_s$ where each $M_s$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $a_ix_j-a_jx_i$ and each $H_s$ is a bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t-m,d-m)$. So $G^\circ$ is obtained by dividing $G$ by $a_0^t$, hence we get $G^\circ=\sum_s H_s^\circ M_s^\circ$, and each $M_s^\circ$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $(a_ix_j-a_jx_i)/a_0$, each of which is in $I_P$. Thus $G^\circ\in I_{mP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Part by part: unit factors in S, unique factorization in R, and for (d) translation of the generic point to the origin plus primariness of powers of a determinantal ideal (Bruns-Vetter).

nodes.name: (a) F and (F^*)° differ by a unit
nodes.statement: (a) Since $F=BF^*/H=B(F^*)^\circ a_0^t/H$, where $t=\deg(H)-\deg(B)$, we see that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by $Ba_0^t/H$, which is a unit in $S$.
nodes.statement_short: (a) F and (F^*)° differ by a unit

nodes.name: (b) a factorization of F^* gives one of (F^*)°
nodes.statement: (b) Note that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by a unit factor in $S$, so one is irreducible if and only if the other is. Also, $F^*$ by construction has no factors of bi-degree $(f,0)$ with $f>0$, so if $F^*$ fails to be irreducible, it factors as $F^*=AB$ where $A$ and $B$ have bi-degree $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$ with $d_A,d_B>0$ and $d_A+d_B=d$. But then $(F^*)^\circ=A^\circ B^\circ$ is a product of factors of positive degree and hence not irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: (b) a factorization of F^* gives one of (F^*)°

nodes.name: (c) factorizations transfer via UFD property
nodes.statement: (c) If $G^\circ$ is not irreducible, then $G^\circ=AB$ where both $A$ and $B$ have positive degree $d_A$ and $d_B$, so we have $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ where $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have bi-degrees $(t_\alpha,0)$ and $(t_\beta,0)$. Since $R$ is a UFD, the denominators in the right hand side of the expression $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ must cancel with factors of the numerators of the expression $\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ and this does not affect the values of $d_A$ or $d_B$, so we may assume that $\alpha,\beta, A^*, B^*$ all are in $R$ and $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a',d_A)$ and $(b',d_B)$, where the simplification might have changed $a$ and $b$ but will have left $d_a$ and $d_B$ unchanged. Since $d_A$ and $d_B$ are both positive, $G$ has nonunit factors so $G$ is not irreducible. Now note that irreducibility of $G^\circ$ implies that for $(G^\circ)^*$ by (b). Finally, by construction, if $G$ is irreducible with bi-degree $(t,d)$ where $d>0$, then $G=c(G^\circ)^*$ for some nonzero $c\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$, hence $(G)=((G^\circ)^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: (c) factorizations transfer via UFD property

nodes.name: (d) F^* lies in J_{mP}
nodes.statement: (d) Since $F\in I_{mP}$, by (a) we have $\frac{F^*}{a_0^s}=(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$, where $(s,d)$ is the bi-degree of $F^*$, and since $d$ is the degree of $(F^*)^\circ$ and since $(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$ we have $d\geq m$. Now let $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= F^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)=\frac{F^*(a_0,\ldots,a_n,x_0,\ldots,x_n)}{a_0^sx_0^d},$$ so as a rational function $D$ has bi-degree $(0,0)$, but as a polynomial in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}]$, $D$ has degree $\delta\leq d$. Moreover, since $x_0\not\in I_P$, we have $D\in I_{mQ}$ where $Q$ is the point $Q=(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})$ in the affine open subset $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})^n$ away from $x_0=0$. Now translate $Q$ to the origin; i.e., consider $$H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big).$$ Note that $$a_0^{s+d}x_0^dH=a_0^{s+d}x_0^dF^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)=$$ $$F^*\big(a_0,\ldots,a_n,a_0x_0,a_0x_1+a_1x_0,\ldots,a_0x_n+a_nx_0\big)\in R$$ is a bi-homogeneous polynomial of bi-degree $(s+d,d)$. Since $H$ has multiplicity $m$ at the origin (with respect to the variables $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$), $H$ is a sum of terms where each term consists of a monomial in $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$ of degree at least $m$ and at most $d$, times a polynomial in the variables $\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}$ of degree at most $s+d$. Thus each term is of the form $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ where $m\leq \sum_ji_j\leq d$ and $c$ has degree at most $s+d$. Thus multiplying by $a_0^{s+d}x_0^d$ clears the denominators. Translating back we recover $D$; i.e., $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big),$$ but each term becomes $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)^{i_n} =c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{a_0x_1-a_1x_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{a_0x_n-a_nx_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ and multiplying by $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^d$ we obtain $$C(a_0,\ldots,a_n)(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}$$ where $C$ is homogeneous in the variables $a_i$ of degree $s+d$, and $$(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}\in J_{mP}.$$ Thus $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dH\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)= a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dD=a_0^{2d}F^*\in J_{mP}$. But by \cite[Corollary 7.10]{BV}, since $J_P$ is the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix of indeterminates, namely the two sets of variables, the powers $J_{mP}$ are primary for $J_P$. Since no power of $a_0$ is in $J_{mP}$, we see that $F^*\in J_{mP}$.

nodes.statement: (d) Since $F\in I_{mP}$, by (a) we have $\frac{F^*}{a_0^s}=(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$, where $(s,d)$ is the bi-degree of $F^*$, and since $d$ is the degree of $(F^*)^\circ$ and since $(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$ we have $d\geq m$. Moreover, since $x_0\not\in I_P$, we have $D\in I_{mQ}$ where $Q$ is the point $Q=(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})$ in the affine open subset $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})^n$ away from $x_0=0$. Now translate $Q$ to the origin; i.e., consider $$H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big).$$ Note that $$a_0^{s+d}x_0^dH=a_0^{s+d}x_0^dF^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)=$$ $$F^*\big(a_0,\ldots,a_n,a_0x_0,a_0x_1+a_1x_0,\ldots,a_0x_n+a_nx_0\big)\in R$$ is a bi-homogeneous polynomial of bi-degree $(s+d,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Dehomogenize and translate the generic point to the origin

Thus multiplying by $a_0^{s+d}x_0^d$ clears the denominators. Translating back we recover $D$; i.e., $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big),$$ but each term becomes $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)^{i_n} =c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{a_0x_1-a_1x_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{a_0x_n-a_nx_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ and multiplying by $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^d$ we obtain $$C(a_0,\ldots,a_n)(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}$$ where $C$ is homogeneous in the variables $a_i$ of degree $s+d$, and $$(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}\in J_{mP}.$$ Thus $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dH\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)= a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dD=a_0^{2d}F^*\in J_{mP}$. nodes.name: (e) generators of J_{mP} dehomogenize into I_{mP}
nodes.statement: (e) If $G\in J_{mP}$, then $G=\sum_s H_sM_s$ where each $M_s$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $a_ix_j-a_jx_i$ and each $H_s$ is a bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t-m,d-m)$. So $G^\circ$ is obtained by dividing $G$ by $a_0^t$, hence we get $G^\circ=\sum_s H_s^\circ M_s^\circ$, and each $M_s^\circ$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $(a_ix_j-a_jx_i)/a_0$, each of which is in $I_P$. nodes.name: B_{n+1} root systems give unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: It seems likely that the root system $B_{n+1}$, which gives a point set $Z_{B_{n+1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, gives rise to an unexpected hypersurface for each $n\geq 2$, but our verifications of unexpectedness are computational and so are limited to a few smaller values of $n$. We do not have a general proof.
assumptions: the root system $B_{n+1}$, which gives a point set $Z_{B_{n+1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$
conclusions: gives rise to an unexpected hypersurface for each $n\geq 2$

nodes.name: matrix N of conditions
nodes.statement: The idea of the script is to construct the matrix $N$ expressing the conditions imposed on all forms $F$ of degree $d$ by the points of $Z$, together with the conditions imposed for $F$ to vanish to order $m$ at a point $P=[a_0:\ldots:a_n]$ with indeterminate coordinates $a_i$ represented in the scripts with new variables.

nodes.name: matrices Q_1 and Q_2
nodes.statement: We can regard $N$ as consisting of two matrices, $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, where $Q_1$ comprises the top $|Z|$ rows of $N$ and gives the conditions imposed by the points of $Z$, and $Q_2$ comprises the bottom $\binom{n+m-1}{n}$ rows of $N$ giving the conditions imposed by the fat point $mP$. Thus the entries of $Q_1$ are scalars in the ground field, but the entries of $Q_2$ are the order $m-1$ partials of the monomials $b_i$ evaluated at $P$.

nodes.name: rank criterion for unexpectedness
nodes.statement: Then $Z$ has unexpected hypersurfaces of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$ exactly when $$\dim \ker N > \max(0,\binom{n+d}{n}-\ensuremath{\mathrm{rank}}\hspace{1pt}(Q_1)-\ensuremath{\mathrm{rank}}\hspace{1pt}(Q_2)),$$ and in this case the coefficient vectors $c$ of the unexpected hypersurfaces are precisely the nontrivial elements of $\ker N$.
conclusions: $Z$ has unexpected hypersurfaces of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$ exactly when $$\dim \ker N > \max(0,\binom{n+d}{n}-\ensuremath{\mathrm{rank}}\hspace{1pt}(Q_1)-\ensuremath{\mathrm{rank}}\hspace{1pt}(Q_2)),$$
nodes.statement_short: Z has unexpected hypersurfaces iff dim ker N exceeds max(0, binom(n+d,n) − rank Q_1 − rank Q_2); kernel vectors give them.

nodes.name: script output (n,d,m,edim,adim)
nodes.statement: An output of the form $(n,d,m,edim,adim)$ means that there is a hypersurface for $Z$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of degree $d$ with a generic point of multiplicity $m$ (that is a point whose coordinates are variables); the vector space of unexpected forms has expected dimension edim and actual dimension adim (where edim can be negative if the number of conditions imposed by $mp$ is greater than the dimension of $[I_Z]_d$).

nodes.name: universal script
nodes.statement: We will refer to the script below as the {\it universal script}.

nodes.name: universal script (Macaulay2 test for unexpected hypersurfaces)

nodes.name: semicontinuity and random evaluation points
nodes.statement: By semicontinuity, if the script indicates that there is no unexpected hypersurface for a given $Z$, $n$, $d$ and $m$ (by not outputting anything), then there is indeed no such unexpected hypersurface. nodes.statement_short: With a random evaluation point, absence of output is reliable by semicontinuity, but reported unexpected cases may be false positives.

nodes.name: root system A_{n+1} and its point set
nodes.statement: The roots for $A_{n+1}$ are the $(n+1)(n+2)$ integer vectors in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{n+2}$ having one entry of 1, one of $-1$ and the rest 0. We project these into $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ by dropping the last coordinate. Projectivizing then gives a set $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of $\binom{n+1}{2}$ points.

nodes.name: root system B_{n+1} and Z_{B_{n+1}}

We thus have $|Z_{B_{n+1}}|=(n+1)^2$ for the corresponding set of points $Z_{B_{n+1}}\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$.

nodes.name: unique unexpected quartic surface for B_4 with 0-dimensional base locus
nodes.statement: In the case of $B_4$ we get a previously unknown unique unexpected hypersurface. It has degree 4 with a general point $[a_0:a_1:a_2:a_3]$ of multiplicity 4. nodes.name: tangent cones of the cone construction
nodes.statement: As an example we consider the tangent cones for the cone construction of \S\ref{cone section}. Assume $Z$ is a finite set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}}$ and that the space $V\subset [S]_d$ of forms vanishing on the points has the property that there is (up to multiplication by a scalar) a unique form $F\in V$ with a point of multiplicity $d$ at a general point $P=[a_0:\ldots:a_n]\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Applying an idea similar to that of Remark \ref{need fewer pts}, remove points if necessary so that we are left with a subset $\{P_1,\ldots,P_r\}$ of $Z$ of $r=\binom{d+n}{n} - \binom{d-1+n}{n} -1$ points. (Now $F$ is not unexpected.) Then $F^*\in R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n][x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ and by Lemma \ref{StEx}(d) $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(\delta,d)$ with $\delta\geq d$. Let $M_j$ be an enumeration of the monomials in $T=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ of degree $d$. Let $m_i$ be an enumeration of the monomials in $T$ of degree $d-1$. Let $t=\binom{n+d}{n}$ and $s=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$. Let $\Gamma$ be the matrix whose top $r$ rows are the values $M_j(P_i)$ of the monomials $M_j$ at the points $P_i$, and whose next (and bottom) $s$ rows are the values $(m_i\cdot M_j)(P)$, where as above the dot indicates the action of $T$ on $T$ by partial differentiation. Note that the entries of $\Gamma$ are all in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n]$. Elements in the kernel of $\Gamma$ are coefficient vectors for forms vanishing at the points $P_i$ and having a point of multiplicity $d$ at $P = a$. The assumption that there are $r=t-s-1$ points $P_i$ and that there is (up to multiplication by scalars) a unique form vanishing on the points with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $P$ means that $\Gamma$ is a $(t-1)\times t$ matrix whose rank at a general point $P$ is $t-1$. Since the entries of $\Gamma$ are monomials of degree 0 or 1, we can divide the $s$ rows having degree 1 monomials by $a_0$ and obtain a row equivalent matrix $\Gamma'$ with entries in the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)$. The kernel of $\Gamma'$ has dimension 1, and for any nonzero vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_t)$ in the kernel, we can take $F$ to be $F=\sum_iv_iM_i$. Note that $(F^*)^\circ$ (and hence $F^*$) also are in the kernel, and so can be used in place of $F$ and thus all have the same tangent cone for a general point $P=a$. Each entry of $v$ is in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}$ so computing the tangent cone gives $$\sum_j \frac{((M_j\cdot F)(P))M_j}{c_j}=\sum_{i,j} \frac{((M_j\cdot v_iM_i)(P))M_j}{c_j} =\sum_i v_i\frac{((M_i\cdot M_i)(P))M_i}{c_i}=\sum_i v_iM_i=F.$$ I.e., $F$ is its own tangent cone, which for a general point $P=a$ is thus defined by $F(a,x)=0$ (or equivalently $F^*(a,x)=0$). We can also work over $R$. Let $\Gamma'^*$ be the matrix obtained by appending $(M_1,\ldots,M_t)$ as a row at the bottom of $\Gamma'$, and let $\Gamma^*$ be the matrix obtained by appending $(M_1,\ldots,M_t)$ as a row at the bottom of $\Gamma$. Then $G'=\det\Gamma'^*$ is a multiple of $F$ by a scalar in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}$ and we have $a_0^sG'=G=\det \Gamma^*\in R$. Since $G'=G/a_0^s$ is a scalar multiple of $F$ by a scalar in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}$, it follows that $G^*=F^*$. Moreover, we have $G=C(a)G^*$ where $C(a)$ is a polynomial describing for which points $a$ the matrix $\Gamma$ has less than full rank. (Suppose that we choose a point $a=Q_1$ such that there is a point $x=Q_2$ for which $G^*(Q_1,Q_2)\neq0$. Then $C(Q_1)=0$ if and only if $\det \Gamma^*=G(Q_1,Q_2)=0$, which occurs if and only if the maximal minors of $\Gamma$ all vanish; i.e., $\Gamma$ has rank less than $t-1$.) As before, $G$ is its own tangent cone, but it's still not clear what $F^*$ is or how $F^*(a,x)$ is related to $F^*(x,a)$. Now assume that there is an irreducible variety $W$ of degree $d$ and codimension 2 such that for a general point $P=a$ the locus $F(a,x)=0$ is precisely the union of all lines through $P$ and a point of $W$, and that $F(a,x)$ is irreducible (and hence so is $F^*(a,x)$ by Lemma \ref{StEx}). Then we have $F^*(a,x)=\pm F^*(x,a)$. Here's why. For a general point $P'=[a_0':\ldots:a_n']$ of $F(a,x)=0$ (and hence of $F^*(a,x)=0$), $P'$ is on the cone through $W$ having vertex $P$, so $P'$ is on the line through $P$ and a point $w\in W$. But then $P$ is on the line through $P'$ and $w$, so $P$ is on the cone $F(a',x)=0$ with vertex $P'$ (hence on $F^*(a',x)=0$), so $F^*(a',a)=0$. I.e., $F^*(a',a)=0$ if and only if $F^*(a,a')=0$. Thus the loci $F^*(a,x)=0$ and $F^*(x,a)=0$ intersect in a nonempty open subset of $F(a,x)=0$. Since $F^*(a,x)$ and $F^*(x,a)$ are irreducible, we have $F^*(a,x)=cF^*(x,a)$ for some scalar $c$. But swapping variables again gives $F^*(a,x)=cF^*(a,x)$ hence $F^*(a,x)=c^2F^*(a,x)$ so $c=\pm1$. Thus in this case, without resorting to Lemma \ref{StEx}(d), we see $F^*(a,x)$ has bi-degree $(d,d)$ and that the tangent cone to $F^*(a,x)$ at a general point $P=a$ is defined by $F^*(x,a)$ (since here the tangent cone is defined by $F^*(a,x)$ but $F^*(a,x)$ and $F^*(x,a)$ define the same locus).
nodes.statement_short: For the cone construction F is its own tangent cone at a general point, and when the cone is over a codimension-two W one has F^*(a,x)=±F^*(x,a).

nodes.name: BMSS duality theorem
nodes.statement: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting an irreducible unexpected curve $C=C_P$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$. \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] The curve $C_P$ is unique. \item[(b)] Let $F(a,x)\in S=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0}\big)[x_0,x_1,x_2]$ be the form defining $C$ over the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0})$. Assume that the lines dual to the points of $Z$ comprise a free line arrangement. Then $F^*(a,x)$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. Furthermore, viewing $F^*(a,x) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,x_1,x_2][a_0,a_1,a_2]$, $F^*(a,x)$ has multiplicity $m$ in the $a$ variables at the general point $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ (briefly we will say $F^*(a,x)$ has a point of multiplicity $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$). \item[(c)] Assume that $F\in R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,a_1,a_2][x_0,x_1,x_2]$ is any bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$ such that $F(a,x)$ is reduced and irreducible for a general point $a=P$ and has multiplicity $m$ both in the $a$ variables at $a=x$ and in the $x$ variables at $x=a$. Then $F_P(a,x)=(-1)^mF(x,a)$ is the tangent cone at $x=P$ to the curve $F(P,x)=0$ for $a=P$, where $F_P$ is defined in (\ref{def of HP}). \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement:

(b) By Lemma ef{StEx}(d) we know that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\geq m$ and that $F^*$ has multiplicity at least $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$. The conclusion follows from examining a parameterization given in \cite{CHMN} to conclude that $m'\leq m$. Let $\Lambda$ be the product of the forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$. It is not hard to check that there are no unexpected curves for $Z$ with $|Z|<3$, so after a change of coordinates if need be, we may assume $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$. Let $(s_0,s_1,s_2)$ be a syzygy of minimal degree (hence homogeneous of degree $m$; see \cite{CHMN}) for the ideal $(\Lambda_{x_0},\Lambda_{x_1},\Lambda_{x_2})$, where $\Lambda_{x_i}$ denotes the partial with respect to $x_i$; thus $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0.$$ Define $\phi$ formally to be the vector whose components are given by the cross product $$\phi=(\phi_0,\phi_1,\phi_2)=(s_0,s_1,s_2)	imes (x_0,x_1,x_2).$$ Now let $\ell$ be the general line $a_0x_0+a_1x_1+a_2x_2=0$. If $a_2
eq0$, we can parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, where $(t,s)$ are projective coordinates on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^1$, and by \cite{CHMN} $\phi$ defines a birational map from $\ell$ to $C$. Note that, since $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$, then $x_0$ divides $\Lambda_{x_1}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$ and $x_1$ divides $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$, but $x_0$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $x_1$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_1}$. Setting $x_0=0$ in $s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0$ gives $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}=0$$ so $x_0$ must divide $s_0$. Similarly, $x_1$ divides $s_1$. Plugging $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ into $\phi(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ we see from the definition of the cross product that $a_2$ divides $\phi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, and since $x_i|s_i$ for $i=0,1$, we get that $x_i$ divides $\phi_i$ for $0,1$ and thus after the substitution $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ that $a_2$ divides $\phi_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. Let $\psi_i=\phi_i/a_2$. Then $\psi_i$ is bi-homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $a$ variables and degree $m$ in the variables $s$ and $t$. We also get a parameterization of $C$ using the slope of lines through the point $P=a$. This induces an isomorphism from $E_P$ to $C$, where $E_P$ is the blow up of $P$. But $\psi=(\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2)$ induces a birational map $\ell$ to $C$. Composing gives an isomorphism $\ell$ to $E_P$, which is therefore linear. Thus after a change of coordinates fixing $P$ and $x_2=0$, we may assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by $\psi$ is the same as that given by slopes of lines through $P$. In particular, consider the line through the point $(a_1/a_2,a_1/a_2,1)$ with slope $t/s$; in affine coordinates it is $$ rac{x_1}{x_2}- rac{a_1}{a_2}= rac{t}{s}\Big( rac{x_0}{x_2}- rac{a_0}{a_2}\Big)$$ which we can rewrite as $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives the coordinates $a_2t=x_1, sa_2=x_0$ as the parameterization on $E_P$, and we can assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by mapping the point $(t,s)$ on $E_P$ to the point $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ where the line $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$ meets $C$ (away from $P$) is the same point of $C$ as that given by $\psi(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$. Thus the parameterization is such that $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_1(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)],$$ and hence plugging $s=x_0a_2-a_0x_2$ and $t=x_1a_2-a_1x_2$ in to $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ gives $(a_2(x_1a_2-a_1x_2),-a_2(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0a_2-a_0x_1a_2)$, and factoring out the $a_2$ we get $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, each component of which has bi-degree $(1,1)$. So we now have parametric equations for $C$, $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(v):\psi_1(v):\psi_2(v)],$$ where $v=(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-x_0a_2+a_0x_2,a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, so each component of the right hand side has bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. We get the following equations for $C$ (bi-homogeneous of degree $(m,m+2)$): $x_0\psi_1-x_1\psi_0=0$, $x_0\psi_2-x_2\psi_0=0$, $x_1\psi_2-x_2\psi_1=0$. The form $F^*(a,x)$ defining $C$ is a common divisor of these three equations. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\leq m$. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, and since it has a point of multiplicity at least $m$ at $a=x$ but degree exactly $m$, the multiplicity is also $m$. (c) Since $F$ has degree $m$ in the $a$ variables, $F$ defines a curve of degree $m$ with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $a=x$, hence it defines a union of $m$ lines through the point $a=x$. The question remains as to what these lines are. To answer this question, translate the point $a=x$ to the point $[1:0:0]$. Doing this gives us $$G(a)=a_0^mF ig(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0} ig) \in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\Big[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big][a_0,a_1,a_2].$$ In the $a$ variables, this defines $m$ lines meeting at $[1:0:0]$. Thus in the $a$ variables $G(a)$ is a homogeneous form of degree $m$, but now the variable $a_0$, which we can regard as defining the line at infinity, does not appear. Note that neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is a factor of $G(a)$, since if, say $a_1$ were a factor of $G$, then for all choices of $x$, $G=0$ includes the line from $[1:0:0]$ to $[0:0:1]$. Since the point $[0:0:1]$ is at infinity, it is fixed under the translation we employed, so $F(a_0,a_1,a_2,x_0,x_1,x_2)=0$ includes the line from $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to $[0:0:1]$, hence $x_1a_0-x_0a_1$ is a factor of $F$, contradicting the assumption that $C$ is irreducible. Since $a_0$ does not appear in $G(a)$ and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are not factors, we have $G(a)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_ma_2^m$ with $b_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig]$ and $b_0,b_m
eq0$. Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Over an appropriate field extension of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})$ this factors as $h(a_1)=(a_1-h_1)\cdots(a_1-h_m)$. Note that the elements $h_i$ are distinct. If not, then $h$ and hence $g$ has a multiple root, say $h_i$, hence $a_1-h_i$ is a common factor of $g$ and $g'$ (or, taking more derivatives, of $g^{(\mu-1)}$ and $g^{(\mu)}$ if the root has multiplicity $\mu>1$) and thus can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the linear factor $a_1-h_i$ is in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and so divides $g$ over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and hence $a_1-h_ia_2$ divides $G(a)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig][a_0,a_1,a_2]$ and thus $F(a,x)$ as before has a corresponding factor linear in $a$, contrary to assumption. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct. Since by Lemma ef{diffMap} the mapping $f$ expressing the coefficients of $h$ as symmetric functions of the roots $h_i$ has an invertible differential $df$ (the roots being distinct), we can by the inverse function theorem \cite[p.\ 33]{FG} regard the roots $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of the coefficients $b_i/b_0$ of $h$. Since each $b_i/b_0$ is a rational (and so holomorphic) function of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$, we can regard the $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$. The roots $h_i$ give the points at infinity where $G(a,x)$ vanishes. Specifically these are $[0:h_i:1]$. These are unaffected by affine translations, so the points where $F(a,x)$ vanishes on $a_0=0$ are these same points $[0:h_i:1]$. Thus translating back we see $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines through $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ and $[0:h_i:1]$, so the forms defining these lines divide $F(a,x)$. Specifically, we have $G(a)=b_0(a_1-h_1a_2)\cdots(a_1-h_ma_2)$ so $$b_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_1 rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)\cdots\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_m rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)=G(a)/a_0^m= F\Big(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big)$$ translates back to $$F(a,x)=x_0^{m+1}a_0^mb_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_1\Big)\cdots \Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_m\Big)=$$ $$x_0b_0 ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_1 ig)\cdots  ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_m ig)=$$ $$b_0x_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ Consider a point $x=a$ where $b_0x_0
eq0$. Then the branches of $F(a,x)=0$ in a neighborhood of $x=a$ are defined by the vanishing of each factor $\lambda_i(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|$. The tangent line to the branch $\lambda_i(x)=0$ at $x=a$ is defined by $((
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a})\cdot (x_0,x_1,x_2)$. Since $\lambda_i=(a_1-a_2h_i)x_0-a_0x_1+a_0x_2h_i$, the gradient $
abla \lambda_i$ is $$\Big((a_1-a_2h_i),-a_0,a_0h_i\Big)+\Big(-a_2h_{i0}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i0},-a_2h_{i1}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i1},-a_2h_{i2}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i2}\Big).$$ The second term vanishes at $x=a$ so $$(
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(a_1-a_2h_i(x),-a_0,a_0h_i(x))|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ So we see that the tangent cone to $F(a,x)=0$ at a point $P=a$ such that $b_0x_0
eq0$ is defined by the vanishing of $$F_P(a,x)=b_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|=$$ $$(-1)^mb_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|=(-1)^mF(x,a).$$

nodes.statement: (b) By Lemma \ref{StEx}(d) we know that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\geq m$ and that $F^*$ has multiplicity at least $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$. The conclusion follows from examining a parameterization given in \cite{CHMN} to conclude that $m'\leq m$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.1(d) gives bi-degree (m',m+1) with m'≥m

nodes.name: Minimal syzygy of the Jacobian ideal and cross product φ
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be the product of the forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$. It is not hard to check that there are no unexpected curves for $Z$ with $|Z|<3$, so after a change of coordinates if need be, we may assume $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$. Let $(s_0,s_1,s_2)$ be a syzygy of minimal degree (hence homogeneous of degree $m$; see \cite{CHMN}) for the ideal $(\Lambda_{x_0},\Lambda_{x_1},\Lambda_{x_2})$, where $\Lambda_{x_i}$ denotes the partial with respect to $x_i$; thus $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0.$$ Define $\phi$ formally to be the vector whose components are given by the cross product $$\phi=(\phi_0,\phi_1,\phi_2)=(s_0,s_1,s_2)\times (x_0,x_1,x_2).$$
nodes.statement_short: Minimal syzygy of the Jacobian ideal and cross product φ

nodes.name: Parameterize a general line
nodes.statement: Now let $\ell$ be the general line $a_0x_0+a_1x_1+a_2x_2=0$. If $a_2\neq0$, we can parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, where $(t,s)$ are projective coordinates on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^1$, and by \cite{CHMN} $\phi$ defines a birational map from $\ell$ to $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Parameterize a general line; φ maps it birationally to C

nodes.name: x_i divides s_i
nodes.statement: Note that, since $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$, then $x_0$ divides $\Lambda_{x_1}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$ and $x_1$ divides $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$, but $x_0$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $x_1$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_1}$. Setting $x_0=0$ in $s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0$ gives $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}=0$$ so $x_0$ must divide $s_0$. Similarly, $x_1$ divides $s_1$.
nodes.statement_short: x_i divides s_i

nodes.name: Divide by a_2 to get ψ of bi-degree (m−1,m)
nodes.statement: Plugging $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ into $\phi(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ we see from the definition of the cross product that $a_2$ divides $\phi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, and since $x_i|s_i$ for $i=0,1$, we get that $x_i$ divides $\phi_i$ for $0,1$ and thus after the substitution $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ that $a_2$ divides $\phi_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. Let $\psi_i=\phi_i/a_2$. Then $\psi_i$ is bi-homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $a$ variables and degree $m$ in the variables $s$ and $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide by a_2 to get ψ of bi-degree (m−1,m)

nodes.name: Identify ψ with the slope parameterization through P
nodes.statement: We also get a parameterization of $C$ using the slope of lines through the point $P=a$. This induces an isomorphism from $E_P$ to $C$, where $E_P$ is the blow up of $P$. But $\psi=(\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2)$ induces a birational map $\ell$ to $C$. Composing gives an isomorphism $\ell$ to $E_P$, which is therefore linear. Thus after a change of coordinates fixing $P$ and $x_2=0$, we may assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by $\psi$ is the same as that given by slopes of lines through $P$. In particular, consider the line through the point $(a_1/a_2,a_1/a_2,1)$ with slope $t/s$; in affine coordinates it is $$\frac{x_1}{x_2}-\frac{a_1}{a_2}=\frac{t}{s}\Big(\frac{x_0}{x_2}-\frac{a_0}{a_2}\Big)$$ which we can rewrite as $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives the coordinates $a_2t=x_1, sa_2=x_0$ as the parameterization on $E_P$, and we can assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by mapping the point $(t,s)$ on $E_P$ to the point $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ where the line $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$ meets $C$ (away from $P$) is the same point of $C$ as that given by $\psi(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify ψ with the slope parameterization through P

nodes.name: Implicit equations give m'≤m, hence bi-degree (m,m+1)
nodes.statement: Thus the parameterization is such that $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_1(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)],$$ and hence plugging $s=x_0a_2-a_0x_2$ and $t=x_1a_2-a_1x_2$ in to $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ gives $(a_2(x_1a_2-a_1x_2),-a_2(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0a_2-a_0x_1a_2)$, and factoring out the $a_2$ we get $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, each component of which has bi-degree $(1,1)$. So we now have parametric equations for $C$, $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(v):\psi_1(v):\psi_2(v)],$$ where $v=(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-x_0a_2+a_0x_2,a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, so each component of the right hand side has bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. We get the following equations for $C$ (bi-homogeneous of degree $(m,m+2)$): $x_0\psi_1-x_1\psi_0=0$, $x_0\psi_2-x_2\psi_0=0$, $x_1\psi_2-x_2\psi_1=0$. The form $F^*(a,x)$ defining $C$ is a common divisor of these three equations. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\leq m$. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, and since it has a point of multiplicity at least $m$ at $a=x$ but degree exactly $m$, the multiplicity is also $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Implicit equations give m'≤m, hence bi-degree (m,m+1)

nodes.name: (c) tangent cone equals (−1)^m F(x,a)
nodes.statement:
(c) Since $F$ has degree $m$ in the $a$ variables, $F$ defines a curve of degree $m$ with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $a=x$, hence it defines a union of $m$ lines through the point $a=x$. The question remains as to what these lines are. To answer this question, translate the point $a=x$ to the point $[1:0:0]$. Doing this gives us $$G(a)=a_0^mF ig(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0} ig) \in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\Big[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big][a_0,a_1,a_2].$$ In the $a$ variables, this defines $m$ lines meeting at $[1:0:0]$. Thus in the $a$ variables $G(a)$ is a homogeneous form of degree $m$, but now the variable $a_0$, which we can regard as defining the line at infinity, does not appear. Note that neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is a factor of $G(a)$, since if, say $a_1$ were a factor of $G$, then for all choices of $x$, $G=0$ includes the line from $[1:0:0]$ to $[0:0:1]$. Since the point $[0:0:1]$ is at infinity, it is fixed under the translation we employed, so $F(a_0,a_1,a_2,x_0,x_1,x_2)=0$ includes the line from $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to $[0:0:1]$, hence $x_1a_0-x_0a_1$ is a factor of $F$, contradicting the assumption that $C$ is irreducible. Since $a_0$ does not appear in $G(a)$ and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are not factors, we have $G(a)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_ma_2^m$ with $b_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig]$ and $b_0,b_m
eq0$. Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Over an appropriate field extension of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})$ this factors as $h(a_1)=(a_1-h_1)\cdots(a_1-h_m)$. Note that the elements $h_i$ are distinct. If not, then $h$ and hence $g$ has a multiple root, say $h_i$, hence $a_1-h_i$ is a common factor of $g$ and $g'$ (or, taking more derivatives, of $g^{(\mu-1)}$ and $g^{(\mu)}$ if the root has multiplicity $\mu>1$) and thus can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the linear factor $a_1-h_i$ is in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and so divides $g$ over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and hence $a_1-h_ia_2$ divides $G(a)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig][a_0,a_1,a_2]$ and thus $F(a,x)$ as before has a corresponding factor linear in $a$, contrary to assumption. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct. Since by Lemma ef{diffMap} the mapping $f$ expressing the coefficients of $h$ as symmetric functions of the roots $h_i$ has an invertible differential $df$ (the roots being distinct), we can by the inverse function theorem \cite[p.\ 33]{FG} regard the roots $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of the coefficients $b_i/b_0$ of $h$. Since each $b_i/b_0$ is a rational (and so holomorphic) function of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$, we can regard the $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$. The roots $h_i$ give the points at infinity where $G(a,x)$ vanishes. Specifically these are $[0:h_i:1]$. These are unaffected by affine translations, so the points where $F(a,x)$ vanishes on $a_0=0$ are these same points $[0:h_i:1]$. Thus translating back we see $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines through $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ and $[0:h_i:1]$, so the forms defining these lines divide $F(a,x)$. Specifically, we have $G(a)=b_0(a_1-h_1a_2)\cdots(a_1-h_ma_2)$ so $$b_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_1 rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)\cdots\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_m rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)=G(a)/a_0^m= F\Big(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big)$$ translates back to $$F(a,x)=x_0^{m+1}a_0^mb_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_1\Big)\cdots \Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_m\Big)=$$ $$x_0b_0 ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_1 ig)\cdots  ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_m ig)=$$ $$b_0x_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ Consider a point $x=a$ where $b_0x_0
eq0$. Then the branches of $F(a,x)=0$ in a neighborhood of $x=a$ are defined by the vanishing of each factor $\lambda_i(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|$. The tangent line to the branch $\lambda_i(x)=0$ at $x=a$ is defined by $((
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a})\cdot (x_0,x_1,x_2)$. Since $\lambda_i=(a_1-a_2h_i)x_0-a_0x_1+a_0x_2h_i$, the gradient $
abla \lambda_i$ is $$\Big((a_1-a_2h_i),-a_0,a_0h_i\Big)+\Big(-a_2h_{i0}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i0},-a_2h_{i1}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i1},-a_2h_{i2}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i2}\Big).$$ The second term vanishes at $x=a$ so $$(
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(a_1-a_2h_i(x),-a_0,a_0h_i(x))|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ So we see that the tangent cone to $F(a,x)=0$ at a point $P=a$ such that $b_0x_0
eq0$ is defined by the vanishing of $$F_P(a,x)=b_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|=$$ $$(-1)^mb_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|=(-1)^mF(x,a).$$
nodes.statement_short: (c) tangent cone equals (−1)^m F(x,a)

nodes.statement_short: In a, F defines m lines through a=x

nodes.name: Translate a=x to [1:0:0]

Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct.

nodes.name: BMSS duality for unique (possibly reducible) unexpected curves
nodes.statement: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting a unique unexpected curve $C$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$. Let $F(a,x)\in S$ be the form defining $C$ over the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0})$ and assume $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. Then $(F^*)_P(a,x)=(-1)^mF^*(x,a)$ defines the tangent cone to $C$ at $P$.
assumptions: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting a unique unexpected curve $C$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$.
Let $F(a,x)\in S$ be the form defining $C$ over the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0})$ and assume $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$.
conclusions: $(F^*)_P(a,x)=(-1)^mF^*(x,a)$ defines the tangent cone to $C$ at $P$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.5
nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite{CHMN} that $C=C'\cup \Lambda_1\cup\cdots\cup \Lambda_r$ where $C'$ is unexpected for a subset $Z'$ of $Z$ and has degree $m+1-r$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m-r$ where $r=|Z|-|Z'|$ and each $\Lambda_i$ is the line from $P$ to $p_i$ where $p_1,\ldots, p_r$ are the points of $Z$ not in $Z'$. Thus $F=GL_1\cdots L_r$, where $G$ is the form defining $C'$ and $L_i$ is the bi-linear form defining $\Lambda_i$. So we have $F^*=G^*L_1^*\cdots L_r^*$, but $L_i^*=L_i$ and $L_i(a,x)=-L_(x,a)$, so $F^*(a,x)=(G^*L_1\cdots L_r)(a,x)=(-1)^m(G^*L_1\cdots L_r)(x,a)$. The tangent cone for $C$ is the tangent cone for $C'$ union with the lines $L_i$, so we also see that $(-1)^mG^*(x,a)L_1^*(x,a)\cdots L_r^*(x,a)=F^*(x,a)$ defines the tangent cone for $C$.
